blocks.text: The chapter’s call to “seek the things above” is not left as an abstract inward focus. The exhortations that follow describe it in embodied communal conduct: abandoning destructive practices, putting on a renewed humanity, and living across ethnic, ritual, cultural, and legal distinctions without those distinctions defining who belongs. The household instructions then address wives, husbands, children, fathers, and enslaved people within unequal household structures.

Verses 12–17 present compassion, forgiveness, love, peace, the word of Christ, singing, thanksgiving, and action in the Lord’s name as parts of one communal exhortation. The repeated focus on “one another,” shared teaching and singing, and thanksgiving shows that these qualities are meant to shape the community’s common life rather than merely private character.

The instructions to enslaved people in 3:22–25 continue into the next verse, where masters are told to provide what is just and fair because they too answer to a heavenly Lord. Reading the passage across this boundary keeps the extended labor instructions from being treated as the whole of the household address.
